chapter: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
title: First impressions of Europe on the Edgar Hayes tour: Gothenburg and Finland
summary: The tour felt like Alice in Wonderland; the Gothenburg concert hall's acoustics made him play more carefully, and in Finland they were the first Black musicians since Josephine Baker.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Maybe we should just ask you what your impressions were when you went, when you did the first European tour with Edgar Hayes. Did it seem like a new world, a different world?

Oh, definitely. Definitely. It seemed -- I don't know, it seemed like Alice in Wonderland to me. Everything seemed to strange, but I knew that I had a job to do and I wanted to do the job as well as I possibly could, and to leave some kind of an impression of American musicians. That was my main -- being young, I was only 24 at the time, but I had the impression that there was something I had to do, and well, our first concert in Göteborg turned out -- it was so beautiful and the people were so understanding, so receptive, until that inspired me to do things in another manner, not the way that we did them at home. That is an approach to music, because we were exposed at that time to this place where we played, it was like a brand new hall, and it had been built with the wood they make bass fiddles from.
For heaven's sake.

It was called the Concert [Husset] (PHONETIC), and it had acoustics like you had never heard before, and the least little thing you did everyone could hear, no matter where they were in the hall. So that gave me a sense of doing things correctly.
Yes.
It made me watch every move that I made,
Which at home it didn't occur to me so much. I knew what I had to do and I would do it, not paying really fully attention to how the outcome was.
Yeah.

But that gave me an impression that everything had to be perfect, because I thought these people were much more civilized than we were at home, and that they were more attentive and that they appreciated what we were doing more.
So they deserved more.
That's it exactly. I wanted to do everything as perfectly as I possibly could.
Yeah.

So they gave me a new approach. And our tour of toured Sweden with a tremendous success, because we were -- people said that we were the first -- in some parts -- well, Jimmy Lunceford has preceded us, in this tour to Sweden, but he hadn't been to Finland. But when we went to Finland and they said there hadn't been any colored musicians there since Josephine Baker, which was about 25 years before.
For heaven's sake.
So we were the first colored people they had seen for about 23, 25 years.
Fancy that.
So they expected so much, because
Josephine Baker had left such a tremendous impression, to follow her was --
Yeah.
You know, it had to be tremendous.
Yeah.
And that's what we tried to do.
Yes.
And the whole tour seemed to be like that. It was all firsts, you know.
